rv.q: Cracknell's production is viscerally effective where Stenham's adaptation feels soft focus.
Nevertheless, as a brave and peculiar character study, this is extraordinary.
There is a stylish sense of theatre here and the acting shines.
In general, though, I was left puzzled by her use of Miss Julie as a template.
Stenham's take on Strindberg is also a problem. Despite promising bold thinking about inequality, racial prejudice, sexual stereotypes and liberal hypocrisy, it proves colourless and slight.
Put simply, the crisis in Stenham’s version seems disproportionate to the events.
My thoughts then for Director Carrie Cracknell are these: trust your actors; and the writing.

The result is a relatively lightweight entertainment that highlights the skills of its star but could make some viewers wonder whether the National might not have been better commissioning a revival of the original text in its own period.
Whilst this new take on a classic story provokes some interesting thoughts it fails to dig deep enough.
But transporting the play to a “liberal” household — in tolerant London — in the permissive 21st century, pulls the rug from under Strindberg’s play.

cn.t: Stenham's modern update divides critics, with Kirby's performance praised but the production faulted for lacking the political context and depth of previous adaptations.
